Question: So, I understand that you can use a post office or mailing building address for your LLC (when filing for the EIN or registered Agent). Would you have to ask such places if you want to use their address for your own LLC?
Answer: Some great answers are here already, so I won’t repeat them except to say the following: (1) Can you use someone’s address, not your own that you don’t control, such as your Registered Agent’s (RA) address, without their permission? The answer is “no.” This would (a) violate USPS regulations; (b) permit whomever’s address to simply not deliver your mail to you; (c) permit them to report you to the USPS; and (d) most importantly, this could be considered a “fraudulent filing”, allowing a clever plaintiff’s attorney to argue to “pierce the corporate veil” thereby destroying any liability protection you were hoping to achieve with your LLC. (2) If the RA gives you permission to use their address, then can you use it? The answer is still “no,” because see (1)(a) and (1)(d) above. This violates USPS regulations, because any third-party mail receiving agency must abide by the USPS CMRA regulations, and that requires filing out Form 1583. We do a LOT of regular LLC filings and anonymous LLC’s, and we won’t let folks use our RA address for their business address because of (1)(a) and (1)(d) above. It does put us at a competitive disadvantage when so much of our competition does this, but as attorneys, we aren’t paid just to create a LLC, but to make sure it’s done right. Larry.

Question: Is it possible to open an online business from another state than the one in which you would like to open it?
Answer: If I’m understanding your question correctly, it appears you’re wondering whether you can open up a company for an online business in another state than the state you’re currently living in and/or doing business in? If that’s your question, the answer is “yes,” you can do that. However, here’s the issue: You will need to “register” your company in every state that it’s “doing business.” Thus, you need to ask yourself where are you “doing business?” This is a surprisingly hard question to answer, because almost all states are unwilling to advise businesses on what it means to be “doing business” in their state, and instead, have rules on what is NOT “doing business” in their state. In general, simply “doing business on the Internet” without something more, is not enough to say you’re “doing business” in a particular state. If a majority of your business seems to be coming from a particular state, then it becomes harder for you to say you’re not “doing business” in that state. Similarly, if you’re advertising exclusively in a state in an attempt to obtain business in that state, it will be hard for you to say you’re not “doing business” in that state. If any of the following questions apply to you, you should really consider looking more carefully at the law within that state to determine whether you should file your LLC as a Foreign LLC in that state: California has one of the toughest “long-arm statutes” that makes it really hard to avoid saying your NOT “doing business” in California, if you own a company and you are a resident of California. Read this article from the California Franchise Tax Board: https://www.ftb.ca.gov/file/business/doing-business-in-california.html. Given all the above, our general recommendation is one of the following: (1) Method One (Form wherever you want) You can certainly create a company wherever you like, but then foreign file it in your home state if you answer “yes” to any of the questions above. Unless you’re taxing your entity as a “C-Corporation,” you’re probably not going to get any tax savings this way with a pass-through entity, because all the profits/losses will flow through to you. (2) Method Two (Your home state, but cannot be anonymous) Just form a company in your home state. The advantages of forming in another state, i.e. Delaware, are going to be too nuanced and esoteric for 99.9% of the business leaders that read this. If you disagree, then please hire a professional to help you evaluate the issues. The primary advantage to this, is you’re going to save some money. (3) Method Three (Anonymous in your Home State) If you care about anonymity, then do this: YOU - - > (own) an Anonymous LLC in WY or NM as a Holding Company - - > (which owns) a Regular LLC in your Home State as your Operating Company Why? I have a knowledgebase article that talks about this: https://www.l4sb.com/knowledge-base/preserving-anonymity-state-discloses-ownership-information/ NM or WY? The general rule is, if you will be the only owner and want disregarded tax treatment, go with NM. Otherwise, go with WY. Question: Can you convert a voting share to a non-voting share in an existing S-Corp? The goal is to give one partner ultimate authority (like a 51/49 partnership) while maintaining equal ownership (50/50).
Answer: The quick answer is “no.” The reason is that a S-Corp does not permit different levels of ownership. If you do this, you can lose your S-Corp status. And, if you lose that, then things can really become problematic because an entity looses its S-Corp status, it becomes a C-Corp from the date of when the problem occurred. You have options. First, if your entity is a Corporation, then you can switch to a C-Corp. Note that when you do this, you will need to think through the issues and definitely handle your accounting and taxes differently. However, if you can get ahead of this decision (versus losing the S-Corp status), you’ll save a lot in headaches, penalties and back-taxes. Second, if your entity is a LLC, then you can switch your tax status from S-Corp to Partnership. A LLC can be taxed as a Partnership, which permits different levels of ownership as you asked about in your question. Beware, you do need an updated Operating Agreement. Third, if your Corporation or any other type (other than LLC), you can “convert” your entity to a LLC, and then tax it as a Partnership as discussed in the former paragraph. This requires a “conversion,” and there’s a bit of expense (although not too much). Good luck to you. Question: Where should I start my business, Delaware, Wyoming, Nevada, Texas, etc.? Way too much info out there but nothing gives me a clear answer on which is the best state to incorporate your business.
Answer: The first question you should ask yourself is, “Where am I conducting business?” This is actually a complicated question, and to answer that question, ask yourself the following questions: If you’ve answered “yes” to any of the questions above, you’re most-likely “doing business” in that state. This means, whatever company you setup, must be registered in those states you’re doing business. For most people, this means their home state of residence. That leaves two choices: (1) Simply form in your home state (and foreign file that company in any other states you’re “conducting business”), or (2) form in Delaware, Wyoming, Nevada, New Mexico, etc, and then foreign file in your home state (and other states you’re “conducting business”). Now, why would you consider #2? Most likely, because you’ve read some information on the Internet (like you’re doing now), but that information was either wrong or it was confusing. Usually, most folks interest in incorporating in one of these states has something to do with taxes (i.e. “There’s no corporate income tax in WY” or “There are no taxes in NV,” so shouldn’t you form there?). The answer depends on how you’re going to tax the entity. Most folks will tax their company as a “pass-through entity,” versus Subchapter C. The reason is Subchapter C exposes you to “double taxation,” and pass-through entities offer a number of tax benefits, depending on a variety of factors (outside the scope of this question and answer). But what is a pass-through entity? It’s where the profits and losses of the company “pass through” to the owner or owners. What this means is, even though you may have a WY company, the profits and losses of the company flow-through to the owners, no matter where they are located. Do you live in Illinois? Doesn’t matter if you have a WY company, because you will need to report your profits / losses on your IL State and Federal tax return. The fact that your company is registered in WY is of no consequence. So, given all the above, it’s generally best to assume you need to form your company in your home state — unless you have a lot of other things going on — but then you can always “move” your company to another state to take advantage of more sophisticated issues after being properly advised by a competent attorney or CPA. Good luck to you. Larry.

Question: Which is the better business structure for a 1-person consulting business, an LLC or a C Corp?

I’ll address the first question first: LLCs are less expensive to setup, less expensive to maintain and less expensive to teardown later if you decide to close your business. If your current plan is to stay small, such as a one-person operation, then LLC is really the way to go. If, in the future, your accountant, CPA or lawyer recommends you switch to a corporation for some reason, your not stuck with your LLC. Its possible to do an entity conversion in most states, or you can domesticate or merge your LLC into the Corporation in another state. You will have a lot of options, is my point. The one exception to my advice above, is if you’re located in the State of Florida and asset protection is your primary concern. The State of Florida has taken what I view as a poor direction with sole-member LLCs, making charging orders and foreclosures easier than in other states. You’d be better with either a multi-member LLC or a Corporation in the State of Florida (in my opinion), or setup a parent/child setup with a holding company in Delaware or Wyoming so you can try to take advantage of those states Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Acts. In regard to the tax question, C-Corp versus a pass-through entity, that’s really something you should discuss with a tax professional. C-Corps can subject you to “double taxation,” although they provide the only real way to manage your personal income if that’s important to you for some reason (i.e. you’re divorced or on social security, and have reasons to limit your personal income). Good luck to you. Larry.

Question: What should be included in a partnership agreement for a business? What should I know beforehand?
Answer: What should you know before entering into a partnership? Believe it or not, what you should know is less “legal” than more “business”. Question: Do companies own by a holding company have to be limited liability companies? Can a holding company own a sole proprietor business?

The answer is “no.” It can be any of the above “assets” I mentioned above. However, can a holding company “own” a sole-proprietor business? The answer is “no.” Why? Because the “business” is not actually an asset, per se. A sole-proprietor business is an individual working by him- or herself, and that individual owns assets of the business. Can the holding company “own” the assets of a sole-proprietor business? The answer is “yes,” but then it’s really not a holding company any more, is it? It owns the assets of a business that is conducting business, so it becomes an operating company. This comes up a lot for anonymous LLC’s that we setup for folks, where you have a holding company that owns an operating company. The operating company is registered in a state where it’s conducting business or the owner lives, and that company is owned by an anonymous LLC that acts as a holding company. Question: If a mechanic hires a tow truck to move a client's vehicle and the tow company causes damage, is it the business or the tow company that is liable to the client?
Answer: The short answer is both are liable. The longer answer is complicated, as there are several legal doctrines influencing liability. The business hiring the tow company is liable for the harms of its agents (i.e. the tow company) under the laws of Agency. The towing company is liable due to its negligence. Who pays for the lability will depend on the nature of the arrangement / contract between the business hiring the tow company and the tow company itself. In an ideal world, there would be an agreement of some type, indicating who is responsible for damage, who carries insurance, who indemnifies whom, etc. Further, both the mechanic and the tow company would hopefully be incorporated (either a Corporation or LLC), to help limit personal liability of the owners of the company. Forming a company, such as a LLC, is very inexpensive and it’s just not worth conducting business (and handling other people’s stuff, such as a car) without incorporating. Learn more at Form a Limited Liability Company (LLC) | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB). Liability protection is sort of like birth control. No one method is 100% effective, so it’s best to use multiple methods. Insurance alone, will not suffice — for example, insurance won’t cover intentional acts and exclusions on the policy. Larry.

Question: If you are a freelance contractor, is it preferable to be a limited liability company (LLC) or an independent contractor?
Answer: Hi, there. A limited liability company (or LLC) is not mutually exclusive to independent contractor. They are actually two different concepts. An independent contractor is an employment status that depends on a number of factors as determined by the IRS (and your home state, which can be somewhat different from the IRS factors). A LLC is an entity type (versus an employment status), and provides benefits over just being employed as yourself (called a sole proprietorship). Question: Can the 51% shareholder of an LLC make and carry out decisions independent of how the 49% member wants to do things?

First, the power to make decisions are going to be in the Operating Agreement (if there is one), and if there is no Operating Agreement, then whatever the statute says (in the state where the LLC was formed). This is important for two reasons: What I mean by this, is the Operating Agreement defines powers and what requires (and doesn’t require) a vote. The Operating Agreement will also dictate whether a vote requires a majority or unanimous vote. It’s possible some decisions require a majority vote, while other decisions require a unanimous vote. It just depends on the Operating Agreement (or statute). Second, regardless of what the Operating Agreement says, you need to know that many states have protections for “minority owners.” Every state is different, but in general, if a majority owner makes decisions that positively impact the majority owner to the detriment of the minority owner, the majority owner is going to create potential liability for him- or herself. This is a real problem for majority owners, because what constitutes “negatively impact?” I’ve had clients get continually harassed and sued by minority owners, claiming everything they did was positively impacting the majority owner as against the minority owners. It’s hard to give you absolute rules here, but an egregious example would be modifying the Operating Agreement to specifically benefit the majority owner, such as allowing the majority owner to put in an anti-dilution clause for the majority owner, that doesn’t apply to the other owners. Question: What is the best way to structure an anonymous LLC in Arizona?
Answer: Arizona doesn’t permit anonymity, but there is a way around this. It’s basically a “parent/child” setup, where you form an AZ LLC as your Operating Company, and instead of you owning the AZ LLC, you form a second LLC as a Holding Company. This second LLC should be an “Anonymous LLC,” which is simply a regular LLC filed carefully in a state that does permit anonymity, such as DE, NM or WY. Then, you own this second LLC. The structure looks like this: YOU → (own) an Anonymous LLC as a Holding Company → (which owns) a regular AZ LLC as your Operating Company This is how you do it. There are some caveats. First, each LLC needs its own registered agent. Second, each state requires you publish a “physical mailing address” for the company — and AZ requires that such an address is located in AZ. So, you’ll need to figure that out because this address is publicly disclosed. A UPS box (with a street address) will work. You just cannot use a PO Box. You can also use the AZ address for your Anonymous LLC in DE, NM or WY. Note that this strategy works for all states that do not support anonymity, except for OR. OR has passed some stringent laws that do not permit a CMRA (a UPS Box or other virtual mailbox) to be used as a physical mailing address for company filings — you need to actually rent some physical location in OR. Question: Is a contract valid if it releases a party from liability for probable injury?
Answer: If we assume all other aspects of the contract are valid and acceptable, such as “consideration,” then such a contract would not be invalid simply because it releases a party from liability for probable injury (sorry for the use of a double-negative here). Contract law is a very complex area of law, and believe it or not, there is a distinction between a contract being valid but unenforceable versus invalid on its face (i.e. voidable versus void contracts). I would argue simply releasing a party from liability for probably injury does not make a contract void simply because of the fact that it releases a party from liability for probable injury. You COULD have a VOIDABLE contract, if there were other deficiencies in the contract, but such deficiencies aren’t dependent or related to the issue of releasing a party from liability for probably injury. Such deficiencies could include: lack of consideration, undue influence, coercion or threats, party lacks capacity, etc. This is a good question, and is why we recommend business leaders never sign contracts without getting a lawyer involved. Question: I want to start my own video production company. I have a website and I get clients, do I have to register my company?
Answer: Do you **have to register your company?** The quick answer is “no,” as all states permit individuals to operate as a “sole proprietorship” (assuming you’re the only owner). However, did you know that video production is actually a risky business? Why? Because you have a lot of potential liability that can attach to the company, and therefore you personally — if you’re operating as a sole proprietorship versus a properly formed company. The biggest liability comes from third-party liability associated with copyright infringement or invasion of privacy. The copyright problem comes from several angles. First, a client asks you to include specific photos, music or video in a production. If the client doesn’t have a right to this material, you can be liable to the third-party (even if it’s material provided to you by the client). Second, if you’re doing a photo shoot and capture some background music or wall pictures, you could be subject to copyright infringement of those copyrighted objects. Third, I’ve seen clients come back and sue the production company, because the clients said they were expecting the production company to deal with the licensing or otherwise “produce around” copyrighted objects. The invasion of privacy issue comes around, simply because you’re included the likeness of a third-party without their permission. No proper release or permissions. This can even happen from — again — client supplied material. What are the chances you can have a problem with the above? No clue. One of the greatest values of a LLC is “liability protection” which means if there is a catastrophic event to an asset within the LLC (i.e. some of the experiences above), only the assets of the LLC are exposed to liability. Your personal assets, home, other properties are not exposed. An LLC isn’t the only thing you need, of course. You should also have “landlord insurance” on top of your “casualty insurance”. Insurance is great, even an umbrella policy. But, insurance won’t cover “intentional acts.” What is an intentional act? Well, the insurance company will determine that, and I’ve seen insurance companies deny coverage because someone hired an unlicensed and unbonded electrician (not the fault of my client, because the electrician lied about his license — but the insurance company still denied the claim of an electrical fire). As it relates to LLC’s and rental properties, there are some things you need to know: If the LLC is only holding property, and not going to be the property manager or act as a landlord (either because you’re hiring a third-party property manager or you’re going to form a different company to be the property manager), then I would recommend forming an Anonymous LLC to give you the additional protection only an anonymous LLC can give. Form in Delaware, New Mexico or Wyoming. You do NOT need to foreign file this LLC in your local state (where the property is located) because you’re not transacting business in the state (just holding property). See Maintain Your Privacy With an Anonymous LLC | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB). If the LLC is going to be the landlord too, then it’s acting as the property manager and it will be conducting business in the state where the property is. In this circumstance, then I recommend a local LLC (i.e. if you’re located in TX, then form a TX LLC) to own the property. Do you care about anonymity? Then, instead of you owning the local LLC, form an Anonymous LLC to own the local LLC. This will help you with a rental property in almost all states, to remain anonymous as well as give you the liability protection of a LLC. You need to form the Anonymous LLC first, then you need to have someone help you with the local LLC (to keep your name off of it). We do both, of course. Question: Where should I incorporate my business and why?
Answer: Lots of misinformation out there, on “where” you should incorporate. The first priority is, “where are you actually ‘transacting business’?” In each state you are transacting business, the state requires you register your company in that state. For most folks, that means where you live, but there are a lot of folks doing business “online,” and that can mean you have no particular state where your customer is. That isn’t the only test of “where are you transacting business,” however. The problem is, every state has its own rules on what “transacting business” in the state means. For example, if a resident simply owns a company, the great state of California says you’re transacting business in its state. Many states say home-based businesses are “transacting business” in its state, even if you have no customers in that state. The next issue is taxes, but that really only matters if your company is NOT a pass-through entity. I can write a book about this, and I just don’t have the time this Sunday morning to do so. So, I will say this: Just because a state (i.e. like NV, WY or DE) doesn’t have corporate income tax, doesn’t mean your company is not subject to income tax. If it’s conducting business in a state that has corporate income tax, you are required to report your company’s share of its income related to transacting business in a state. Therefore, your DE, NV or WY company will not help you avoid state income tax if you’re conducting business in another state, whether CA, IL, NY, FL, etc. So, you should really consult with a good CPA on this, as well as a business attorney. Question: If a person owns 100% of an LLC company, is he at risk of liability issues?
Answer: The answer is “maybe.” The general rule is that the owners (called members) of a limited liability company are immune from the liabilities of the LLC. There are two important exceptions. The first relate to liabilities an owner agrees to, such as a personal guarantee signed for a lease, bank loan or other liability. When an owner does this, they are agreeing to be personally liable for some debt or obligation of the LLC. The second exception is called “piercing the corporate veil,” which is a legal doctrine that can be used in a lawsuit to hold the owner of a LLC liable for some obligation of the LLC. This can happen in certain circumstances where a plaintiff in a lawsuit claims some sort of “wrong doing” on behalf of an owner of a LLC and that the plaintiff should therefore be permitted to go after the owner to satisfy a gross injustice that would otherwise occur if the plaintiff is unable to seek redress from the owners directly. What constitutes “piercing the corporate veil?” Unfortunately, it does depend on the state where the lawsuit is being held. If they are properly alleged in a complaint, and proven in a lawsuit, owners can be held liable for the liabilities of a LLC for: Some folks will form an Anonymous LLC (see Maintain Your Privacy With an Anonymous LLC | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB)) in an attempt to reduce exposure to a lawsuit. An Anonymous LLC cannot really protect you from a lawsuit and you have the same exposure for “piercing the corporate veil” as a regular LLC, but because ownership information cannot be looked up for an Anonymous LLC, some people feel that acts as a disincentive for plaintiff’s attorneys to accept contingency cases against Anonymous LLC’s. If anyone is blindly advising all startups, regardless of long-term goals and objectives, need for anonymity, tax issues, etc, to form a Delaware C-Corporation; then such people should be ignored. There are a lot of issues that go into not just entity selection (corporation versus LLC) and tax status (C-Corp versus S-Corp versus something else), but also state and choice of forum. The issues are actually quite complex, and there are numerous posts to Quora that address some of the complexities. I’ll tell you just one: Just because you form a C-Corporation in Delaware, doesn’t necessarily mean you don’t have to pay state income tax. You may not need to pay state income tax in the State of Delaware, but you may need to pay state income tax in your state of residence or where you’re actually conducting business. Name: Larry Donahue
Question: What are some of the disadvantages of an LLC?
Answer: I think context is important to this question. Specifically, as compared to what? As compared to doing business as a sole-proprietorship or partnership? The answer here is: not a lot of disadvantages. There are some practical headaches that some business owners may not be used to with a LLC, versus doing business as a sole-prop or partnership, such as filing annual reports for the LLC (depending on the state) or following “formalities” as specified in the Operating Agreement to call votes on important decisions. There are also some minor differences in how you keep your books, open up and maintain bank accounts, etc. These are purely administrative in my opinion, but I find that administrative burdens (even small ones) can be overwhelming for some business owners. If you think this could be you, my advice would be to hire a business bookkeeper or business lawyer to guide you or make sure you doing things correctly. Or, as compared to doing business as a corporation? The answer here is: There could be some tax disadvantages, as compared to a corporation, depending on a few issues. Specifically, Trump’s Tax Reform Act of 2017 sort of brought Corporations back into fashion by providing for some tax advantages only available to corporations, not LLC’s (despite the tax status of the LLC). I’m not a tax professional, so I cannot weigh in on the specifics. We did create a rather sophisticated AI-based business entity selection tool (still in beta), that factors the tax issues, if you’re interested. It only takes 5 minutes: Business Entity Selector Tool | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB). Another disadvantage of a LLC over a corporation, is that you cannot go public with a LLC and some investors (i.e. VC’s) will only invest in corporations and not LLC’s — although this last part is becoming less pronounced, as more and more VC’s are becoming comfortable investing in LLC’s. Finally, you cannot have a non-profit LLC. All non-profits (that I’m aware of) or corporations (because of the board of directors you need). LLC’s are the only entities that can provide anonymity I will say that many business owners are told by their accountants to “form S-Corp,” but usually when an accountant says that, they mean “Subchapter S” so a LLC can fit the bill. LLC’s are the only entities that permit the owners to conduct business anonymously. Learn more at: Maintain Your Privacy With an Anonymous LLC | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB). Good luck to you. Larry.

Name: Larry Donahue
Question: Can a Canadian Ontario Corp run payroll (issue W2s & 1099) for its US residents employees. If so what does it need in US to do that? EIN#? Bank account? Address (physical or virtual?). Or does it need to have a Corp (Delaware or any other) to do so?
Answer: This is a great question. The quick answer is “yes,” a Canadian company can hire US-based resident employees. The question is “how.” (What I’m about to say applies to W2-based employees, not 1099-based employees.) The Canadian company (or any company located outside the US) must first “domesticate” in the United States. It does this by filing a foreign entity filing in the state (or states) it is doing business. Typically, this means where you have W2-based employees, at a minimum. If you’re “generally selling stuff on the Internet,” and selling to all 50 states, that does not mean you need to file in all 50 states. But, if you have a W2 employee in NY and IL, then it means those two states. If you’re selling services or products primarily to a large customer in PA, then it means that state, too. My law firm offers low-cost, flat-rate fees for foreign filings, but it does depend on what type of entity you have. You did say “Corp” above, so here’s our link for foreign corporations: Foreign Corporation Registration | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB). Once you have at least one foreign filing in the US, you will need to get a FEIN. In order to do that, you will need to indicate a “Responsible Party” to the IRS who either controls or owns (even partially) the company. That Responsible Party must have a FEIN (for another company), a SSN (for a US-based citizen) or a ITIN (for anyone issued an “International Taxpayer Identification Number). With the FEIN, you can then do withholding and more. It is NOT necessary to have a US-based bank account. Depending on the state where you foreign file, you may or may not need a US-based address. The general rule is: It can be located anywhere, but it cannot be a PO Box. There are at least three states that don’t follow this general rule: AZ, OR and CA. For AZ and CA, you can use a “virtual address” located in the state. For OR, the legislature there are complete fools, and they won’t even permit a virtual address. In order for you to comply with their “doing business in the state” laws, they require you to actually rent or lease space on behalf of the company. I’m hoping some one will sue the State of Oregon, because they are being absolutely ridiculous. You do NOT need to form an actual corporation in the US. The foreign filing is sufficient. Larry.

Question: From a tax perspective, what is the best way to add a member to my LLC to create a partnership?
Answer: Here is my recommendation on how to add a new member to your LLC, to convert your LLC from a Sole Member LLC to a Multi-Member LLC thereby creating a partnership. Step 1: Verify you really like this new partner, and that they will add value to the organization. After all, you’ve been operating as an individual and responsible to no one. This will be like a marriage. You better love your partner, and your partner better bring value commensurate with the ownership percentage. Can you trust them? Will they be up-front about conflicts of interest? Do they take “the high-road?” How do they behave, when they think no one is watching? Step 2: Verify your goals and objectives, responsibilities and create SMART Goals (Read more: S.M.A.R.T. Goals are Smart to Have | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB)). Put them on paper. Step 3: Talk to (1) a CPA or Accountant, who can explain the best way to handle the new partnership from a tax perspective, and the best way to bring someone on. Step 4: Talk to (2) an attorney, who can write up a good Operating Agreement (that serves as a partnership agreement), possibly put in a Buy/Sell Agreement or Employment Agreement or other relevant documents, depending on how you want things structured. DO NOT: Promise an ownership stake in your company, without writing it down, and letting the guy or gal work for you or with the company, until you have the documents finalized. I’ve had to defend too many businesses in “partnership disputes,” dispute the fact that paperwork was never signed and the parties could never agree on anything. Question: Should I have an umbrella LLC with multiple rental LLCs, each LLC own single property?
Answer: This is a common strategy to help limit liability exposure. It helps to create “silos of exposure,” and is a valid way to reduce risk. Otherwise, if you have all your property in one LLC, and you have a “catastrophic event” in one property, you expose the entire portfolio of properties. Because you’re renting property, you have the risk of a catastrophic event (i.e. fire that kills a tenant, for example). As an attorney, I’ve literally seen it all: murders, fires, children getting electrocuted because wires were damaged and exposed without landlord’s knowledge, and (believe it or not) a car plowing right through a rental property. The quick response from many folks is, “that’s what you have insurance for.” The problem is, insurance doesn’t cover intentional torts. We had one client who hired an electrician out of the Yellow Pages, claiming he was licensed and bonded, and sure enough he wasn’t. That opened up a number of problems for the client, including the insurance company refusing coverage for a fire that started due to the substandard electrical work. From a tax perspective, I am not an accountant so I cannot refute what Carol Kayes is saying, but it’s my understanding that all the “property LLC’s” can be disregarded, with all profits and losses flowing up to the parent LLC (what you call the umbrella LLC), and if you tax that as Subchapter S, that’s what you report. Do check with your accountant on this, though, and I will tell you this is standard practice for many large property owners. One other benefit, if you do it right, is anonymity. Many landlord don’t want to be harassed by their tenants, and so opt for an anonymous LLC as their umbrella LLC. We do this all the time. If you want anonymity, then you need to hire someone to do it for you (to keep your name off the paperwork), and you need assistance with the property LLC’s. For more info on Anonymous LLC’s, go to: Form an Anonymous LLC | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB) For more info on help with property LLC’s, go to: LLC Formation | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB) Thank you and good luck. Larry.

Name: Larry Donahue
Question: How can one convert an LLC into an S corp?
Answer: When I’m asked this question, it is often because a business owner was requested to do this by a CPA / Accountant. The problem is, “S-Corp” is very ambiguous and it’s very important to understand what the CPA / Accountant is requesting. Specifically, is the CPA / Accountant requesting to change your company’s tax status with the IRS to “Subchapter S”? If so, this is a very easy thing to do. Or, is your CPA / Accountant actually requesting you change the type of entity from a LLC to a Corporation (taxed under Subchapter S)? If so, this is more difficult. To accomplish the first, you need to simply submit an entity tax designation change with the IRS. I believe that is ISR Form 8832 or 2553. To accomplish the second, that is much harder. Depending on the state where domesticated, you can either do an “Entity Conversion” from LLC to Corporation, or you can do a Merger. Both request special forms and documents to be submitted to the State, as well as obtaining new formation documents (i.e. Bylaws, shareholder agreement, etc), and making sure you call a vote and do the proper procedures to “approve it”. You also need to notify your banks, folks you contract with, etc, because you are no longer YOUR COMPANY, LLC, but instead YOUR COMPANY, INC. You may need to change letterhead, signs, legal notices, etc, depending on where you have “LLC” listed or displayed. You really need to treat it as a formal “project,” and revise everything everywhere as appropriate. If you do not do this, you risk losing your liability protection by permitting a plaintiff to pierce the corporate veil (because they will argue you are fraudulently conducting business by misidentifying your entity type). Can you tell that I get bugged by CPA’s / Accountants who either do this for their clients themselves, or make such requests without being very specific? I deal with this a lot. We provide Anonymous LLC’s to folks (see Maintain Your Privacy With an Anonymous LLC | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB)), and their accountants will later tell them, “You want a S-Corporation.” The problem is, of course, all the above — and we cannot maintain anonymity with a Corporation, only a LLC. So, I invariably have this conversation a lot. :-) Larry.

Name: Larry Donahue
Question: How's an LLC's member ledger changed when new member is added, if working by percentage? How do you handle decreasing the % of existing members?
Answer: The short answer to your question is: Double-check what the Operating Agreement says, and if you have no Operating Agreement, then you need to look to the statute. In general, it works as follows: It’s a math problem. Who is “selling” the ownership? A particular Member or the LLC itself? If the Member, then only that Member’s percentage ownership decreases the exact amount of the ownership percentage he or she sold. The selling member gets to keep the proceeds of his or her sale. This is only permissible, of course, if the Operating Agreement (or Statute) supports this and/or that Member followed the right process. If the LLC itself is selling the ownership interest, then the purchasing Member gets the percentage he or she acquired. The remaining members are reduced, pro rata, according to their percentage ownership interest. For example, if you had two Members originally, one owning 33.33% and the other owning 66.67%, then the one who owns the 66.67% share gets hit twice as hard. I’ll give you some numbers to illustrate how this works: Originally: 50% & 50%, new member comes on board taking 33%. New: New member has 33%, original members both decreased equally (you can literally multiply their ownership % by the new member’s ownership percentage, then subtract, to get the answer). Original members now own 50% - (50% * .33) = 33.5% each. Second example: Originally: 25% & 75%, new member comes on board, taking 25%. New: New member has 25%. Original 25% member now has 25% - (25% * .25) = 18.75%, other 75% member now has 75% - (75% * .25) = 56.25%. Clear as mud? We do a lot of Anonymous LLC’s (see Maintain Your Privacy With an Anonymous LLC | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB)), and this very problem comes up a lot. Our clients end up bring on new partners, changing owners, etc. I will say, make sure you have a strong Operating Agreement, and when you do sales like this, make sure you have a good “Membership Interest Purchase Agreement.” Good luck to you. Larry.

Name: Larry Donahue
Question: What is best way to prove the ownership in the Delaware C-corp?
Answer: Great question, because I get this question a lot — whether you’re talking about a LLC or a Corporation. The reason I get it so much, is that we do so many Anonymous LLC’s (See Maintain Your Privacy With an Anonymous LLC | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB)). The point of an Anonymous LLC is to protect the identity of the owners, and our clients often wonder how they prove ownership if their name is not listed at the Secretary of State’s Office. So, the short answer to your question is: The stock certificate or purchase agreement or other document evidencing your ownership (for LLC’s, that would be an Operating Agreement). That is the “best” (and only) way to prove ownership. The longer answer is, company ownership is not like buying a piece of real property (that is recorded with a deed) or a titled asset like a car. There is no “title” per se, and the state doesn’t keep track of it that way. It would be too complex, burdensome and costly. As a result, any and all information at the Secretary of State’s Office is always outdated and inaccurate. They have no way to verify identity of the owners. Therefore, for those states that do require ownership information, they are just a formality. They are not verified, and criminals and malfeasants will still lie to the SOS’s office about who owns the company. Typically, however, most folks just don’t keep it up-to-date, and even with states that have annual reporting requirements — you’ll find the information is often a year or more out-of-date. Therefore, contracts and other documents evidencing ownership is necessary. Can such documents be forged? Of course. Can someone forge the bylaws and stock certificate of Apple Corp, and try to take over one of Apple’s billion-dollar bank accounts? Sure, someone can try, but that would be criminal activity, and banks and other financial institutions have processes and procedures to prevent a stranger from walking in and taking over an existing bank account. This does create problems for sole owner companies or those companies with a only a few owners, and something happens to the primary owner. It can often take a court order (or at least proof of death or other significant documents) to add a new signer to a pre-existing account where the previous signer doesn’t also authorize this. I hope this has answered your question. Larry.

Question: Can I have an LLC without making the director's name public?
Answer: It is possible to own a LLC, and not have your name disclosed publicly. We do this all the time for investors, wealthy individuals, former abuse victims and folks trying to go into business without alerting former employers or others. We call this an “Anonymous LLC,” and you can learn more here: Maintain Your Privacy With an Anonymous LLC | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB). It’s not just a matter of “picking a state,” however. I couldn’t disagree with Lewis’ answer more (and his spreadsheet is wrong for many states, but I won’t get into that). You need to ask yourself, “where are you transacting business?” This question is more than where your customers are. Where are you living? Where do you have W2 employees? Where do you have a “base of operations” or “store inventory.” Typically, you will be “transacting business” in the state you live, even if you’re just selling stuff online. You need to register your company where you are transacting business. If you live in a state that requires disclosure of members or managers, then you have a problem. You cannot simply form a LLC in DE, NM or LLC. You need to a bit more work, to ensure your name is not disclosed in your home state. In such circumstances, we recommend you create two companies. The first company is an operating company in your home state, and the second is an anonymous LLC acting as a holding company, whose sole purpose is to own the operating company in your home state. It sort of looks like this: You → (own) an anonymous LLC as a holding company → (which owns) a local LLC as your operating company In order to do this right, you need to have a third-party set this all up for you. This is because you want to avoid having your name be identified as the Organizer or Registered Agent. The holding company will be listed as a sole member for the local operating company. Clear as mud? You can learn more about this here: Regular LLC versus Anonymous LLC | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB). Good luck to you. Larry.

Name: Larry Donahue
Question: Where should I form the LLC?
Answer: Here’s the roadmap in trying to figure out which state to form your LLC: (1) First, are you “transacting business” in the state you’re a resident? If so, then you need to either (a) form the LLC in your home state, or (b) form in another state, but then register the LLC in your home state. What is “transacting business” in your home state? Unfortunately, each state has different rules and regulations about this — and all states don’t tell you what IS transacting business in the state, they just tell you what isn’t (i.e. having a bank account, holding property, etc). What I can tell you, is that it’s more than “where is your customer.” Typically, if you have a W2 employee (including yourself), or you have a “base of operations,” or a retail location, or keep inventory, or you otherwise “avail yourself of state resources,” you are generally considered “transacting business” in your state. If you are, then the state needs to know about it. We have a low-cost, flat-rate service to form a LLC anywhere: Form a Limited Liability Company (LLC) | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB). (2) Second, if #1 above isn’t an issue, then do you care about anonymity? If you care about anonymity, your options are limited. Only a few states permit anonymity, with Delaware, New Mexico and Wyoming being the most popular. However, if you live in Alabama, Colorado, Georgia, Idaho, Iowa, or Virginia, you can also have an anonymous LLC, so you’re back to your home state. Learn more: Maintain Your Privacy With an Anonymous LLC | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB) (3) Third, if #1 and #2 aren’t issues for you, then will you want to tax your LLC like a C-Corporation? If so, again, your options are limited. Specifically, I am only aware of Delaware and Wyoming as not having corporate income taxes. Some folks will say Texas or Nevada, but that’s not true because they both have “gross receipts tax” (so does Ohio and Washington), which are arguable worse than income tax. Between Delaware and Wyoming, I think Wyoming is better, because Delaware has a rather high franchise tax / fee. Wyoming is much more reasonable. Form a WY LLC now: LLC Formation | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB). (4) Fourth and finally, if none of the above area issues for you, then is cost-savings an issue for you? If so, we have a very similar analysis as #3 above. Wyoming is cheaper than Delaware. However, if you think you may or could be “doing business” in your home state, registering in either state is just adding additional expense and complexity. You’d be better served just forming your LLC in your home state. (5) If none of the above, then form in your home state. I hope this is helpful for you. Note that there are a lot of nuanced issues I have not covered above. The above are just “the biggies” that most people seem to ask me about. You would always be best served asking a local business lawyer their opinion, given your unique circumstances. Good luck! Larry.

Question: How can you operate an LLC in two different states? How should you set it up?

Name: Larry Donahue
Question: What is the best way to structure the sale of an LLC (partnership) from a tax perspective?
Answer: The best way to structure the sale of an LLC taxed as a partnership depends mostly on what side of the transaction you’re on. In our blog article titled, Two Common Ways to Buy an Existing Business | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB), we discuss some of the pros and cons of asset sales and stock/ownership sales. As a general rule, if you’re the seller of a business, you usually want to minimize the amount of gain you need to pay taxes on. Selling your ownership interest in the company is often the best way to do that. Your gain would be the excess of the sale price over your basis in the ownership interest, and most (if not all) of those gains will be treated as capital gains and taxed at the lower capital gains rate. A percentage of the gains may be treated as ordinary income depending on the percentage of the LLC’s assets that are “hot assets” like unrealized receivables or inventory items. By contrast, if you sell the assets of the company, your gain is the excess of the sale price over your basis in those assets. This can be especially problematic if you’ve depreciated those assets over the years, as you might be looking at a lot of taxable gain – and maybe even depreciation recapture income, which does not enjoy capital gains rates. In short, sellers usually prefer ownership interest sales to asset sales. From a buyer’s perspective, buying the assets of the LLC usually makes the most sense from a tax perspective. When you buy an ownership interest in a company, your basis in that ownership interest is what you paid for it – but the company’s tax basis in its assets remains unchanged. If the company depreciated its assets before you bought the company, you won’t get to re-depreciate them later. However, if you buy the company’s assets, your basis in those assets is what you paid for them – and you can then depreciate those assets over a term of years, resulting in significant tax deductions. One important factor to consider is that an LLC taxed as a partnership can only remain taxed as a partnership when the LLC has multiple members. If an individual buys the entire ownership interest of a multi-member LLC, the “partnership” is effectively dissolved during the transaction. This produces a very odd result that the IRS addresses in Revenue Ruling 99-6. In this situation, the sellers of the LLC are treated as having sold their ownership interests and can treat it as the sale of a capital gain (to the extent there aren’t hot assets involved). The buyer, meanwhile, is treated as having purchased the assets of the LLC following dissolution of the partnership, with basis allocated amongst the LLC’s assets in accordance with Internal Revenue Code Section 732(c). This situation can prove favorable for both the buyer and the sellers, though the buyer might still prefer an asset purchase because the buyer will have more control over how to allocate the purchase price amongst the different assets which, in turn, affects the amount and timing of depreciation deductions. To summarize, sellers usually prefer to sell their ownership interest, buyers usually prefer to buy assets, and selling a multi-member LLC to a single buyer will generally (though not always) result in both sides enjoying preferential tax treatment. In any event, you should always consult with a qualified tax attorney or accountant about your unique situation to ensure you’re getting the best tax treatment possible. Buying and selling a company isn’t a zero-sum game, and there are ways to structure these deals that benefit everyone in some way or another.

Question: Is it legal to allow somebody else to use my signature?

You also see some form of this with powers of attorney (POA) or limited powers of attorney, or with a personal representative (to an estate) — but in both instances, it’s best of the POA or Personal Representative sign with their own name, and then identify who they are and their authorization for signing on someone else’s behalf. Name: Larry Donahue
Question: What’s the process of being a shareholder of a private company?
Answer: That’s a great question, and there are actually a surprising number of steps to do this correct. I wrote a blog article a few years ago that goes into quite some detail about this (Read it here: Tips for successfully joining a partnership | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB)). The quick summary is there are three components: Due diligence, evaluating and the simple mechanics of becoming a shareholder. Due diligence means you need to actually look at the formation documents (i.e. to make sure you have proper powers, things aren’t too one-sided, etc), the financial health / strength (i.e. so you’re not inheriting debt, liabilities or risk you weren’t aware of), and the tax issues. Different companies will have different due diligence needs (i.e. a chemicals company would be different from a medical practice, in terms of licensing, permitting, insurance, etc). Evaluating means you determine if things are as you understand them to be, that everything is fair-and-balanced between the shareholders, the shareholders get along and collaborate in the best interests of the company, etc. You also owe it to yourself to talk with a CPA to understand the tax implications of your becoming a shareholder (i.e. if you’re not careful, you can suddenly find yourself with a huge tax bill, depending on how you become a shareholder). Are you “buying in” or just receiving shares? If the former, how will that money be used? Are you “buying” from the company or a particular shareholder? If you’re just receiving shares, what is the company (and your position) actually worth? Are you prepared to pay taxes on ordinary income associated with this “gift?” Finally, the simple mechanics usually means you sign some form of “purchase agreement” for your shares, which may also include a “buy/sell agreement” and other documents related to your agreement with the company or other shareholders. You may or may not be issued stock, depending on how the company handles this. This is just a QUICK overview. If this company has any value, or you’re being asked to pony-up any money at all, you really should consult with a local, competent business attorney to guide you. Good luck! Larry.

Question: What is meant by competent to a contract?
Answer: Hard to say, without more context or detail to your question. If “competent” is actually the word you meant to type, then perhaps you mean “competent to enter into a contract?” If so, then competence relates to capacity, as in, “does one possess capacity to enter into a contract?” Capacity relates to a number of issues, including competency. Minors lack capacity to enter into a contract. Mentally disabled persons lack capacity to enter into a contract. “Protected adults” (i.e. adults who lack mental cognitive functions to understand what they are entering into) lack capacity. Even intoxicated or persons under the influence of a mind-altering drug could be said to lack capacity to enter into a contract. It’s just not related to the capacity of the person. It could relate to the capacity of a company or its agent. The laws of agency are very complex, but not just anyone can lock a company into a contract. Persons without the proper authority could be said to lack capacity. If you’re concerned about a particular contract, it’s best if you consult with a properly licensed contracts attorney. My firm provides a $10/page (min. 5 pages) flat-rate contract review. To learn more or order, go to the following link: Flat-Rate Contract Review (Limited) | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB). Thank you and good luck to you! Larry.

Question: Can a contractor take both government and civil contracts?

Question: What does LLC mean?
Answer: “LLC” is an abbreviation for “limited liability company.” A limited liability company, or LLC, is a type of corporate entity that is favored by smaller and medium-sized organizations because of its low-cost, simplicity and ease of maintenance over time. LLC should be contrasted with a “corporation,” which is also another form of corporate entity. Corporations are generally considered “more formal” corporate structures, and therefore a bit more costly and a bit more difficult to setup and maintain. There are vast differences between the two types of corporate entities or structures, and you should consult with a business attorney to determine which is best for you. The answer generally varies on whether you intend to go public some day, what state you would form in, your tax preferences and more. For more information, you may be interested in our two links. For LLC’s, go here: Form a Limited Liability Company (LLC) | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB). For Corporations, go here: Form a Corporation | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB). Thank you. Larry.

Question: What are the ways that differentiate a contract from a mere agreement and why does the law make the distinction between them?
Answer: I’m a bit confused by the question, so let’s make sure we’re speaking the same language. When you say “agreement” versus “contract,” are you meaning one document that can be legally enforceable versus another document that cannot be legally enforced? If that’s what you mean, then a “legally enforceable” contract generally requires a “bargained for exchange of value”. There are many exceptions, however, to what would be otherwise considered a legally enforceable contract, including (but not limited to) one party lacks capacity (i.e. a minor or protected adult), duress/coercion, against public policy, no specific term, etc. There are also exceptions where something could be legally enforceable, even though you do not have all the elements required to comprise a contract (i.e. offer, acceptance, consideration, etc). One exception would be “detrimental reliance.” Not all the states have the same definition for this, but in general, if one party “detrimentally relied” on the statements or actions or inactions of another party, to his or her detriment, there are circumstances when this could be enforceable.

Question: Can an LLC registered in Delaware in the USA have two business accounts at 2 different banks in the USA?
Answer: Yes, companies can have as many bank accounts, with as many banks, located in whatever states (or countries) as they wish. A company is not limited to banks in the state for which it was formed (i.e. a DE LLC is not limited to DE banks). The only issue, is that to open a bank account, you will need a FEIN and to obtain a FEIN you will need to disclose a “Responsible Party” who either (1) controls the company, or (2) is a owner in the company, and has either a SSN (i.e. US Citizen), FEIN (i.e. another US company), or a ITIN (i.e. a foreign national). Question: Will an LLC license be right if I want to start a financial service company all on my own?

Question: Can my US incorporated company give stocks to someone in Russia?
Answer: Hi, there. The general answer is “yes,” although there are some entity types (i.e. S-Corporations) that are restricted by the types of owners it can have. In particular, S-Corporations (or LLC’s that elect Subchapter S tax treatment) may not have foreign owners. So, if you have a Corporation, is it a S-Corporation? If so, then the answer is “no.” If your Corporation is a C-Corporation, then the answer is “yes.” Similarly, if you have a LLC and it’s taxed under Subchapter S, you will lose your tax designation under Subchapter S with a foreign owner. You can, however, change the tax election of the LLC to “partnership” or Subchapter C. Bringing on a foreign owner is not without consequences, depending on the structure and tax status of your company. You will need to consult with a CPA for tax issues. Also, if you will be transmitting significant amounts of cash to or from your Russian partner, you may need to abide by certain federal reporting requirements (I am not well versed in such laws, so cannot comment on them here). Finally, my law firm sets up many “anonymous LLC’s” for businesses, many of the owners are offshore. These LLC’s not only permit foreign ownership, but keep ownership information off the public lists. To learn more, check out this link: https://www.l4sb.com/services/business-formation/anonymous-llc/. Hope this was helpful. Good luck. Larry.

Question: How do you become released from an auto renewal contract?
Answer: Hi, there. This can be easy or it can be hard, depending on the wording of the auto-renewal clause (also called “Evergreen Clause”). The big issue, is that you want to terminate the evergreen properly, and this can be tricky. If you don’t abide by the language properly, you can lose your opportunity to terminate. In particular, does the language require notice of termination “within” or “before” a certain timeframe? Make sure you understand the language, and make sure you can provide evidence that your notice of termination is timely. Note the reverse is true, if you wish to invoke an option to extend the contract. I’ve been involved in circumstances where a party (i.e. a building owner who has a land lease) was late in invoking their optional right to renew by a just a few days, and therefore lost millions of dollars real estate because their 50-year land lease expired. If you feel the language is ambiguous, contact a contracts attorney to help you. Good luck to you! Larry.

Question: How do I add members to a member managed LLC in Texas?
Answer: Hi, there. The answer to this depends, and can potentially be complicated. I’ll give you two processes, depending on the circumstances of the Company: (1) Brand new company, and the new member is a founder? You can probably simply add that new member to the initial Operating Agreement. (2) Existing company? Follow these steps: (i) Review the Operating Agreement, and make sure you follow the formalities about adding a new member (usually calling a vote). (ii) Put together a Purchase Agreement that indicates how much of an interest they are buying, with any restrictions, and any / all disclosures that may be appropriate (i.e. not registered with the SEC, significant liabilities, restrictions on ownership, etc). (iii) Amend the Operating Agreement, at least adding the new member, but it may be a good time to review and revise as appropriate. (iv) Signing party. Some things to consider: Consult with a CPA if the LLC has any value, and if you’re transferring membership for a value of anything other than the fair market value of the ownership being transferred. If the new member is an employee, you should really think through the issues, and add provisions in the purchase agreement for vesting / reverse vesting and/or clawback if employment should be terminated for cause or employment ends within a period of time you think is unreasonable. There are other caveats, so you would do yourself (and your LLC) well by quickly consulting with a properly licensed business attorney in your jurisdiction. Good luck to you. Larry.

Question: Can a company be funded even before its incorporation?
Answer: The answer is “yes, but not a good idea.” You can certainly use your own funds or the funds of other founders to kick-start efforts. You can also obtain loans in furtherance of the company. The problem if you do this, is that because the company technically doesn’t exist, it’s really you (or the other founders) that is actually borrowing money. And, in many instances, it may be difficult or impossible to transfer the liability of any loans from yourself personally to the company. Another problem can result between founders: If founders start putting in money, and there’s any disagreement about the amounts or ultimate ownership percentages, you’re going to have a big problem later. Therefore, given how inexpensive it is to incorporate (i.e. our rates start at $275 plus filing fees), why would you wait? See: Form a Limited Liability Company (LLC) | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB) It is less risky to put the company together first, and then put the right paperwork together to support whatever funding arrangements you seek. Good luck to you! Larry.

Question: If I incorporate a holding/conglomerate company, will I have to incorporate all subsidiaries separately or are they automatically incorporated?
Answer: I’m a bit confused by your question, because you really cannot have a “holding company,” if its not incorporated — you own it as either a sole proprietorship or within a partnership. You or the partners actually own everything. Same goes for the subsidiaries. So, I’m going to assume when you say “incorporate” you mean both the holding and subsidiaries are currently owned by you as sole proprietorships or partnerships. If that’s the case, if “incorporate the holding company,” then the holding company is incorporated but the subsidiaries are probably going to still be held by you as sole proprietorships or the partnership. What you need to do, is make sure you transfer whatever you’re calling a “subsidiary” into the corporation (the holding company) or create new corporations that are the subsidiaries, and then make sure the holding company owns the subsidiaries. This is very complicated, and depends very much on the nature of your assets and how everything is set up. Therefore, with all due respect to the other posters to this question, you really need to consult with a properly licensed business attorney. Good luck to you. Larry.

Question: Hello everyone: I formed LLC registered in Florida in 2016, but the company have no activity yet: do I have to make the anual report with form 1065?
Answer: Hi, there. I think you may be mixing up two issues: “annual report” versus “federal income tax filings.” The “annual report” is with the State of Florida, and the Form 1065 is the IRS income tax form for a “partnership,” such as a LLC taxed as a partnership where K-1’s are issued and passthrough income flows through to the owners. The annual reports are due “between January 1 and May 1 each year”. To learn more, go to: File Annual Report. You need to do this, whether you had activity or not. Form 1065, if your LLC is being taxed as a partnership, is due March 15th, unless you file an extension. If you obtained your FEIN for your LLC as a sole proprietorship, it’s likely your LLC is being taxed as a disregarded entity. You should double-check your SS-4 when you obtained your FEIN, if you obtained your FEIN. Again, you need to do this, whether you had any financial activity or not. In both instances, penalties apply if you file late or don’t file at all. Good luck to you. Larry.

Name: Larry Donahue
Question: Can you give away equity or membership interest to investors in an LLC without adding anyone to the actual LLC?
Answer: Good questions, and I receive this often from entrepreneurs. Can you provide a “membership interest” without “having their name on the actual LLC?” It really depends on the state and what you mean by “having their name on” the LLC. My comments are: If someone has a “membership interest” in a LLC, such as an investor, by definition they are a part owner of the LLC. If your state requires disclosure of all owners of the LLC, then you will have to disclose the investor as a member of the LLC. Fortunately, you will not have to do this until your next annual or biannual report is due (depending on your state), and there are options to obfuscate members information. For example, by asking your investor to obtain an Anonymous LLC (see Maintain Your Privacy With an Anonymous LLC | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB)) and then the Anonymous LLC is the member of your LLC, not the investor personally. Can you “give away” interest without “giving them voting power”? I’m going to assume you don’t actually mean “give away,” since the investor will be buying an ownership interest in return for paying the LLC cash. The question then becomes, can a LLC issue a “non-voting class” of ownership? The short answer is “yes.” This takes a bit of work, because you need to develop a strong Operating Agreement that maintains at least two classes of ownership, with the rules, policies and procedures for such classes. This is fairly common, for example, when LLC owners permit deceased members’ families or estates to maintain an ownership interest in the LLC — they will define non-voting interest for such members. With that said, I doubt most (sophisticated) investors will permit their investment to be a non-voting interest. If you have such an investor — that’s great for you — it implies to me they are friends or family or unsophisticated at some level. Either way, I want to caution you to do this right. You need to put together other documents, aside from a strong Operating Agreement. You need a “Membership Interest Purchase Agreement” for investors, that not only defines what type of class of ownership they are purchasing, but contains a slew of disclaimers, representations, etc. You may also want to consider a “Restriction Agreement,” and perhaps a “Buy/Sell Agreement,” depending on where you’re going with your business and your overall goals and objectives. The problem for you is, if you do this without being careful, you can create what I call a “lose-lose situation” for yourself. If the business tanks, you can open yourself up to personal liability from such investors. If the business succeeds, you can open yourself up to a challenge on ownership, value and class of ownership. If you’re “investor” will be employees or contractors, you have other issues to contend with. Good luck to you. Larry.

Name: Larry Donahue
Question: Where do I incorporate my s-corp? Legalzoom? Rocketlawyer? Can I do it in person and cheaper?
Answer: As Jeremy said, you can do it yourself. Before you do, I have some questions for you: are you sure a “S-corp” is the best entity type for you and your business? Are you simply looking for “s-corp” tax treatment, and a LLC could suite your needs? Do you have family, friends or third-parties as partners? The “LegalZoom’s” of the world are nothing more than “document filers,” and will simply do as you ask. If you don’t know the answers to the above, or you have partners, it’s very doubtful you’re going to get the right documents to support the partnership. For example, if you do go with a S-Corp and you have partners, you would do well to have a “Buy/Sell Agreement” put together with the other documents, to properly address the issue of a partner wanting to leave in the future. I cringe when I see statements that say, “I’ve heard of other people using LegalZoom in the past, and it’s been fine.” The problem with that statement, is it’s really easy to setup a company. It’s much harder to setup a company that works well for the owners in the long-term. I know this is an extreme analogy, but it helps illustrate the problem: If you’re planning a mission to mars, you don’t measure success of the mission simply on whether the rocket left the launch pad successfully. Question: What's the difference between anonymous member LLC and non-anonymous one?
Answer: In general, most states (with only a few exceptions) require you to report who is either a Manager or a Member of the LLC. A Manager does NOT need to be a member. So, you can create an Anonymous LLC in your home State, if you (1) form a Manager Managed LLC, and (2) disclose the name of the Manager. Then, your members will be “anonymous,” although you will have a public Manager. The downside with this, is that you have a public Manager. Their name is disclosed. And, the Manager actually “manages the LLC,” and you therefore need to be very careful about your Operating Agreement, so that the Member(s) delegate power appropriately, and have the proper rights to change the Manager as appropriate. Note that such states also require filing of annual or biannual reports (and some even require “initial reports), and if you think you’re getting away with a level of anonymity by changing things after you register your LLC, you’re just going to have to tell the State how things are once your reports are due. The three states were we form truly Anonymous LLC’s are Delaware (DE), New Mexico (NM) and Wyoming (WY). They do not require disclosure of Manager(s) or Member(s). So, the difference between an “Anonymous Member LLC” and a non-anonymous one is whether you have to disclose the Manager or Members, and how you do it. Just FYI: Another way to create an Anonymous LLC is to form a parent LLC in one of the states that permit Anonymous LLC’s, and then have that parent LLC form a LLC in your State. When you disclose who is the Manager or Member of your State’s LLC, the answer is the parent Anonymous LLC. This is perfectly legal and will help you maintain anonymity for the local / child / transacting LLC in your State. We help lots of clients do this, and the benefit of having a law firm do this versus just anyone on the Internet, is that you receive competent advice from an attorney, as well as “attorney/client privilege” and “attorney/client confidentiality.” Other non-law firms simply cannot provide that. What it means for the LLC’s we form, is that we do not respond to subpoenas unless they have authority over us, and those that do, we’ll first attempt to quash such subpoenas. It also permits you (or your attorney(s)) to raise attorney/client privilege in certain legal proceedings, which may or may not be helpful to you depending on the circumstances. To be clear, attorney/client privilege and attorney/client confidentiality are not absolute. There are limitations. Learn more at: Maintain Your Privacy With an Anonymous LLC | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB) Thank you. Larry.

Question: What is a bill of sale and how is it legally binding?
Answer: When we use a “Bill of Sale” in a transaction, it is usually accompanied by a “Purchase Agreement” of some type, among other potential documents, including promissory note, corporate formation documents (i.e. revised ByLaws or Operating Agreement), etc. A Bill of Sale is a legal document, but I hesitate to actually call it a “contract” for the purchase of personal property (as opposed to real estate). The reason is, a Bill of Sale is usually a very simple document that outlines the purchase price, and sometimes (not always) enumerates “what is purchased.” The “what is purchased” part is usually a high-level list of what is purchased (such as in a business transaction) that separates into IRS taxable categories. What you won’t find in a Bill of Sale, are the general terms of the sale, such as conditions precedent (i.e. what has to be in place before the sale takes place), representations and warranties (i.e. that the seller has good title, hasn’t encumbered the property being sold, condition of assets, etc), payment terms, closing date, etc, etc, etc. I tell my clients to think of the “Bill of Sale” as a “receipt” more than the contract regulating the transaction or purchase. Given it’s simplicity, there really isn’t much to enforce. If it’s the only document in the transaction, you better hope it has enough specificity to fully identify the transaction to make it enforceable. If it doesn’t have enough information, we need to fall back to other aspects of contract law, including but not limited to the Parol Evidence Rule, Detrimental Reliance, etc, to determine whether we can introduce additional evidence to make a legal argument to enforce a Bill of Sale, especially if there was some form of detrimental reliance on behalf of the buyer (i.e. paying money) or seller. Larry.

Question: How do I update Consulting Agreement with compensation?
Answer: If you were advised by a lawyer then I think you should follow the advise of that lawyer versus “double-check” or whatever it is you’re doing on the Internet with this question. With all due respect to the previous two responses, one isn’t quite right and the other didn’t really seem to answer your question. What your lawyer said is right on the money. There are two issues here: First, maintaining the right to even use or incorporate the code into whatever you’re doing. Second, taking full ownership in the copyrights of the code, if that’s important to you. Currently, you’re busy creating a “derivative work” by using that code base — and do you know who owns that derivative work? You guessed it — your former consultant. You asked “how do you update Consulting Agreement,” and your question obviously implies you have a document and you want to update it. I hope you can understand it’s very difficult to tell you how to update something without seeing it. The best answer is to have that lawyer you talked to originally revise your document for you. In my opinion, you really don’t need a “Consulting Agreement” for what you’re trying to accomplish. What you want is some form of “IP Rights Assignment” or something similar. You’re simply purchasing either a license to use (and transfer, display publicly, and make derivative works) of the code you have, or you are purchasing the full copyrights. Your document needs to be very specific: What are you purchasing (i.e. A license? If so, to what extent? The full copyright as defined in US Copyright law?) for what (i.e. The code developed by Consultant from date X to date Y, on the platform Z, along with all notes, data models, structures, etc, etc, etc)? Include any representations and warranties necessary (i.e. he hasn’t assigned his rights to a third-party, he won’t dispute or challenge this agreement, etc, etc, etc). It’s a funny thing about contracts. Universally, they are either a complete waste of time (because there was never an issue, the business didn’t go anywhere, or there was simply no value in “the deal”) or they are utterly important and viewed as the best investment you’ve ever made (because there was a big dispute, or the value became astronomical and you were able to enforce your rights). Most people don’t like to spend money on writing a good contract, and I get it, but to be perfectly honest, almost 50% of my firm’s revenue comes from what I call “dispute resolution” associated with trying to either defend a poorly written contract (yes, downloaded from the Internet) or representing the other side getting out of a poorly written contract. It’s hard to predict for my clients, but spending a few hundred to get a well-written contract really outweighs the tens-of-thousands they spend in a legal battle because the contract was poorly written. Some of my clients end up loosing vast sums in investments, because they didn’t properly lock down their rights, only to see valuable code or other assets be taken out from under them (this is very common with software and other Intellectual Property). Okay, I’m off my soap-box. Good luck to you! Larry.

Question: What happens if you register your company LLC and after 2-3 months you just want to stop, close, or whatever? What do you do?
Answer: This is actually more complicated that it seems. First question, do you have any partners / co-owners? If yes, then do all your partners / co-owners agree with the dissolution? If yes, then draw up a simple “separation agreement” or “dissolution agreement” by and between the partners / co-owners. If you’ve answered “no” to “do all partners / co-owners” agree, then you need to follow the requirements of dissolution in your formation docs (i.e. the Operating Agreement). Second, once you have all the formalities worked out, i.e. what to do with any contributions, outstanding assets, liabilities, etc, then you apportion as agreed. Third, follow your state’s dissolution requirements. This is usually the submission of an Articles of Dissolution, but in many states, you may need to do more, including getting a tax certification from the relevant tax department, etc. Your mileage will vary, depending on the state. Fourth, as mentioned by other posters, you still need to file your final tax returns. Good luck to you! Larry.

Question: Is it possible to name my LLC different from my website name or product? Is it legal (Florida)
Answer: I have to respectfully disagree with the other answers on this post, only because your question was very specific: Can your “brand name” be different from your “legal name”. The answer is yes, but Florida has what’s called a Fictitious Name Statute (see more at: OnLine Fictitious Name Registration) which means you need to register (and pay a fee) for the use of such brand names. Brand names, such as your website name or names for your product, are considered “fictitious names” if different from the actual legal name of your company. Therefore, if you are using one or more fictitious names, you are required to register such fictitious names with the State of Florida. See the link I posted in the previous paragraph. Note you’re required to post it in at least one local newspaper. Good luck to you. Larry.

Name: Larry Donahue
Question: When starting a firm that operates in many states, what considerations do you take into account when deciding how to incorporate (LLC vs. S-corp)?
Answer: I receive this question, or various forms of it (i.e. “I’m starting an e-commerce company that only does business online”), pretty much on a daily basis. Mr. Rigotti, a CPA below, indicated you should consult with your CPA first. That’s a good idea, because the primary decision point for you is going to be your tax position and setting up the appropriate tax structure for your business. For example, if you’re the only owner, most CPA’s will advise you to consider a Corporation taxed as an S-Corporation versus a LLC, usually because a sole-member LLC is taxed as a disregarded entity. So, my advice is to FIRST talk to your CPA to ascertain what entity type would hold the greatest tax advantage for you. THEN, ask your CPA about the multi-jurisdictional tax issues you could potentially be faced with, depending on your business model and structure. I’ll give you some examples, to illustrate the issue. Suppose you form a company in Texas and you do business just in Texas. You will need to deal with Texas tax issues. What happens, however, if you open up a store in Oklahoma, and you’re still doing business in Texas? Do you have to pay state taxes in OK and in TX? The answer is complicated — you pay taxes according to the amount of business you do in each state. A CPA can help you understand the issues. Now, suppose you’re “doing business in” (or operating in) many states? How do taxes work? To answer this question, you need to answer “what does doing business in” a particular state mean? Are you really doing business in a state, just because a resident of a state went to your website to buy something? The answer is usually no, but there are exceptions. At the end of the day, it helps to determine what states you’re truly “operating in,” and then figure out how your tax situation would play into that. You may need to consult with your CPA and your business lawyer to really get a good handle on this. For example, if you’re not doing business in CA, assuming you meet that state’s tests for “not doing business in” the State of CA, you probably don’t want to worry about CA — because CA corporate filing fees and franchise fees can be expensive. ONCE you figure all that out, then forming the company, whether Corporation or LLC, is rather straightforward. Remember to file in those states you’ve decided you’re truly operating in, as a Foreign LLC or Corporation. Good luck to you. Larry.
